properties.name: Ephesus
properties.notes: Ephesus headed the conventus Ephesius, the grandest of Asia's assize districts, and the proconsul heard civil and criminal cases in its Odeon and State Agora. Pliny the Elder counted it among nine cities of Asia that held court and ranked it the brightest light of the province. Litigants from Lydia and Ionia converged on its docket rather than wait for the governor's slower stops elsewhere. Serving as advocate before the Ephesus court was a mark of civic prestige.

properties.name: Pergamon
properties.notes: Pergamon headed the conventus Pergamenus, one of nine Asian assize towns Pliny the Elder named as seats of justice. The proconsul convened court beneath the Attalid acropolis, hearing cases from Mysian and Aeolian communities across the district. Pergamon was also famed for medicine and its royal library, lending its court sessions added prestige. The assize drew litigants who otherwise rarely saw a Roman magistrate face to face.

properties.name: Smyrna
properties.notes: Smyrna headed the conventus Smyrnaeus, one of nine court towns Pliny the Elder named in Asia's assize system. The proconsul held sessions in a city famed for its gridded streets and busy harbor, hearing disputes carried from Ionian coastal towns and inland Lydian communities alike. Smyrna competed openly with Ephesus and Pergamon for primacy in the province, and its assize sessions were part of that rivalry for prestige. Litigants often arrived by sea rather than by the inland roads.

properties.name: Sardis
properties.notes: Sardis headed the conventus Sardianus, a district Pliny the Elder counted among Asia's nine great court towns. As the former capital of Lydia's kings, it hosted the proconsul near its temple of Artemis, hearing suits from towns across the Hermus valley. Sardis later ceded part of its territory when nearby Philadelphia split off into its own assize. Even so, Sardis kept its rank as one of the busiest stops on the governor's circuit.

properties.name: Miletus
properties.notes: Miletus headed a conventus Milesius attested since the Roman Republic and still active under the Flavian emperors. A governor's inscription from that era assigned at least five neighboring cities, including Magnesia on the Maeander, to bring cases to Miletus. The proconsul convened court near a harbor that had once launched dozens of Greek colonies. Smaller Ionian and Carian towns saved a long trip to Ephesus by having Miletus as their assigned seat instead.

properties.name: Halicarnassus
properties.notes: Halicarnassus headed a Carian assize district created after Rome stripped nearby Mylasa of conventus status following a devastating raid in 40 BC. The proconsul heard cases in the city where Mausolus once built a tomb ranked among the ancient world's seven wonders. Halicarnassus absorbed several of Mylasa's former dependent towns into its own docket, widening its reach along the Carian coast. Its harbor made the city a convenient stop on the governor's circuit of Asia's southwestern district.

properties.name: Alabanda
properties.modern_location: near Doğanyurt (Araphisar), Çine, Aydın Province, Turkey
properties.notes: Alabanda headed the conventus Alabandensis, a Carian assize district already flourishing when Rome organized the province of Asia around 50 BC. The proconsul held court in the city's bouleuterion, the same hall Alabandan citizens used for local government, hearing suits from towns across the Marsyas valley. Alabanda was known across the ancient world for its dark local marble and gem-like stones. Litigants from smaller Carian communities converged there for the governor's annual visit.

properties.name: Apamea
properties.notes: Apamea, refounded on the site of Phrygian Celaenae, headed the conventus Apamensis, serving litigants from deep in the Anatolian interior. The proconsul held assizes in a city astride the trade route to the coast, the same standing that made it host to the 188 BC peace treaty between Rome and the Seleucid Empire. Its theater and civic inscriptions recorded generations of business alongside the governor's sessions, a lifeline for inland Phrygian towns far from the sea.

properties.name: Synnada
properties.notes: Synnada headed the conventus Synnadensis, a Phrygian assize district Pliny the Elder named among the nine court towns of Asia. The proconsul convened sessions in a city famed for the honey-and-purple marble quarried nearby at Dokimeion and shipped across the empire. Litigants from the mountainous Phrygian interior traveled to Synnada rather than cross the province to the coast. Its inland position made the assize one of the harder stops on the governor's route.

properties.name: Cibyra
properties.notes: Cibyra gave its name to the conventus Cibyraticus, though court sessions were actually held at Laodicea on the Lycus, the most prominent of roughly twenty-five member cities. Pliny the Elder recorded the arrangement, noting Laodicea's rise even as the district kept Cibyra's older name. Cibyra itself stayed wealthy, famed for gladiatorial games and swift horses, visible in its large theater and mosaic-floored odeon. A district named for one city but run from another was a genuine oddity.

properties.name: Adramyttium
properties.notes: Adramyttium headed the conventus Adramyttenus, the assize district covering Asia's northwestern corner across Aeolis and the Troad. The proconsul held court in a coastal city founded in the sixth century BC, hearing cases from towns across the plain of Thebe. Its harbor linked the courtroom to sea traffic bound for Troy and the Hellespont. A ship out of Adramyttium later carried the apostle Paul partway toward Rome, a sign of how the port tied local business to the wider empire.

properties.name: Cyzicus
properties.notes: Cyzicus headed the conventus Cyzicenus, one of eleven assize districts Sulla organized in Asia after defeating Mithridates in 85 BC. The proconsul convened court in a Mysian port wealthy enough to petition the Senate directly over its own privileges, a request preserved in an inscribed decree. Built on an isthmus joined to the mainland by two bridges, the city gave Rome's judges a base on the Sea of Marmara, its assize surviving swings between free-city status and provincial control.

properties.name: Philadelphia
properties.notes: Philadelphia sat inside the conventus Sardianus for its first century under Roman rule before becoming the seat of its own assize district. A Flavian-era inscription still listed it under Sardis's court, so the promotion came sometime in the second century, on a date the record never pins down. Founded around 189 BC by King Eumenes II of Pergamon, the city bridged Lydia and Phrygia. Whether its own court had opened by Trajan's death in 117 CE simply went unrecorded.

properties.name: Cadiz
properties.notes: Gades headed the conventus Gaditanus, the westernmost of Baetica's four assize districts, seated in a port city that predated Rome itself. Phoenician traders from Tyre founded Gadir around 800 BC, and after siding with Rome against Carthage the city rose to allied status before Julius Caesar granted its citizens full Roman citizenship in 49 BC. Its native son Lucius Cornelius Balbus became the first foreign-born consul in Roman history, proof of how far Gaditane wealth and connections reached into the Senate itself. Fishermen and garum merchants along the Atlantic coast brought their disputes to a court that felt as much like a trading floor as a Roman tribunal.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.7 (conventus lists of Baetica)

properties.name: Cordoba
properties.notes: Corduba headed the conventus Cordubensis and doubled as the seat of Baetica's governor, making it the political capital of the entire province. Rome founded the colony in 169 BC on the Guadalquivir, and its river port anchored a district that swallowed the silver and copper workings of the Mons Marianus to the north, ground overseen by an imperial procurator answerable directly to the emperor. The city later produced the philosopher Seneca and his nephew the poet Lucan, evidence of a court culture rich enough to send its sons to Rome for the highest offices. Litigants from mining camps and river towns alike converged on a bench that mixed metal claims with the ordinary business of a provincial capital.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.10 (conventus lists of Baetica)

properties.name: Ecija
properties.notes: Astigi headed the conventus Astigitanus, the smallest of Baetica's four assize districts but among its wealthiest, refounded as Colonia Augusta Firma around 14 BC. The proconsul held court in a city built on olive money: river barges called lyntres worked the Genil down to the Guadalquivir loaded with amphorae stamped by Astigi's own potters, bound for legions on the Rhine. That oil trade left a physical monument in Rome itself, filling part of the broken-pottery hill of Monte Testaccio. Litigants here argued shipping contracts and production disputes as often as the crimes an assize usually handled.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.11 (conventus lists of Baetica)

properties.name: Seville
properties.notes: Hispalis headed the conventus Hispalensis, the Baetican assize seated where the Guadalquivir stayed navigable for seagoing ships. Scipio Africanus took the city from Carthage in 206 BC, and Julius Caesar later raised it to colonial status as Colonia Iulia Romula. The proconsul's court sat inside a river port so central to Baetica's export trade that the word portus came to be applied almost exclusively to warehouses and workshops tied to Hispalis's docks. Olive oil, wine, and grain converged there from across the province before crossing the Atlantic route to Rome, and the litigation the assize handled followed that same money.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.11 (conventus lists of Baetica)

properties.name: Tarragona
properties.notes: Tarraco headed the conventus Tarraconensis and doubled as capital of the entire province, the largest territorial command in the Roman world, covering roughly two-thirds of the Iberian peninsula. The Scipio brothers fortified the city in 217 BC at the opening of the Second Punic War, prompting Pliny the Elder, who served here as procurator in 73 CE, to call it "Tarraco, the Scipios' work." Augustus himself governed the empire from Tarraco for nearly two years while recovering from illness after the Cantabrian Wars, running imperial business by courier from its forum. Litigants at the governor's own assize competed for attention with the machinery of an entire province, since Tarraco's court and its capital functions shared the same forum.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.18-21 (conventus lists of Tarraconensis)

properties.name: Cartagena
properties.notes: Carthago Nova headed the conventus Carthaginiensis, a district whose reach stretched far inland to the silver-bearing Meseta rather than staying hugged to the coast. Hasdrubal Barca founded the city around 227 BC as a Carthaginian stronghold, and Scipio Africanus seized it in 209 BC along with the mines that had drawn Carthage there in the first place. Strabo counted some 40,000 workers laboring the district's silver veins at their Republican peak, and though the richest deposits were largely exhausted by the second century CE, the assize's docket still carried mining leases and boundary disputes inherited from that industry. Its natural harbor kept the court's business flowing even after the ore ran thin.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.25; Strabo's Geography 3.2.10

properties.name: Zaragoza
properties.notes: Caesaraugusta headed the conventus Caesaraugustanus, a district Pliny the Elder recorded as embracing 55 separate communities along the middle Ebro valley. Augustus founded the colony around 14 BC on the site of the older Iberian town of Salduie, settling veterans of his Cantabrian campaigns and naming the city for himself. The proconsul's court sat at a crossroads linking the coastal conventus at Tarraco to the interior circuit at Clunia, giving a colony barely a century old outsized traffic through its forum. Free-colony tax privileges did nothing to slow the flow of court business routed through it.

properties.name: Clunia
properties.modern_location: Peñalba de Castro, Burgos Province, Spain
properties.notes: Clunia headed the conventus Cluniensis, covering much of the northern Meseta from a hilltop city sprawled across 130 hectares above 1,000 meters elevation. Colonia Clunia Sulpicia sat astride the roads linking Tarraco, Caesaraugusta, and Asturica Augusta, giving the proconsul a natural hub for a mountainous, thinly settled district. Roman legions stationed nearby proclaimed Galba emperor here in 68 CE, a reminder of how deep Roman military and legal authority reached into the Duero highlands. A winter assize at this altitude was no soft posting for a traveling magistrate.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.26-27 (conventus lists of Tarraconensis)

properties.name: Astorga
properties.notes: Asturica Augusta headed the conventus Asturum, founded near the end of Augustus's reign as a military and administrative anchor for the newly subdued Astures. A road ran straight from its gates to Las Medulas, the largest gold-mining operation in the Roman world, worked by the arrugiae and ruina montium techniques Pliny the Elder described after his own service as the province's procurator. Pliny put the combined output of Asturia, Gallaecia, and Lusitania at 20,000 Roman pounds of gold a year, with Asturia supplying the largest share, and he called Asturica itself a magnificent city. Litigants at its assize argued mining claims and labor disputes thrown up by an industry that reshaped whole mountainsides.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 33.78 (gold output); 3.28 (conventus lists)

properties.name: Lugo
properties.notes: Lucus Augusti headed the conventus Lucensis, the assize district covering Gallaecia's Atlantic coast from the Verdugo river north to the Navia. Pliny the Elder counted 166,000 free persons scattered across the district's fifteen tribal peoples, communities he noted still carried names unfamiliar to Roman ears generations after conquest. The settlement grew up around hot mineral springs the Romans exploited even before the assize was formalized, giving the site its earliest reason to exist. Litigants from Celtic hill communities across Hispania's northwest corner traveled to a proconsul's court seated near the empire's Atlantic edge.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.28 (conventus lists of Tarraconensis)

properties.name: Braga
properties.notes: Bracara Augusta headed the conventus Bracarensis, the southernmost of Gallaecia's three Atlantic assize districts, its territory running from the Douro river north to the Sil. Pliny the Elder recorded 24 constituent civitates and roughly 385,000 free persons under its jurisdiction. Augustus founded the city around 20 BC as a garrison town for the newly conquered Callaeci, and it grew into the road hub where routes from Asturica Augusta, Lucus Augusti, and the Atlantic coast converged. Litigants from scattered hill communities across the district traveled those same roads to reach the proconsul's court.
sources: Pliny the Elder's Natural History 3.28 (conventus lists of Tarraconensis)

properties.name: Merida
properties.notes: Emerita Augusta was Lusitania's provincial capital and the seat of its largest conventus, hearing cases from the wealthiest and most Romanized third of the province. Pliny the Elder named it first of the three jurisdictions when he described Lusitania's court system. Governors and their staff worked from the city's forum, a short walk from the theatre where advocates built their reputations.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Emerita Augusta, Merida · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Santarem
properties.notes: Scalabis, refounded as a Caesarian colony on a bluff above the Tagus, governed Lusitania's western jurisdiction. Pliny the Elder listed it alongside Emerita and Pax as one of the province's three assize seats, drawing litigants from the towns strung along the river toward the Atlantic. A Roman temple podium still standing in the old citadel today marks the civic core its magistrates once worked from.

properties.name: Beja
properties.notes: Pax Iulia governed Lusitania's southern jurisdiction, the district covering the grain- and olive-rich plains toward the Guadiana. Pliny the Elder named it the third of the province's three courts, alongside Emerita and Scalabis. Surrounding villas like the one at nearby Pisoes shipped their produce through the town on the way to the wider Roman market.
